title: Review: Coyote vs. Acme is an unabashed love letter to Looney Tunes
gist: Coyote vs. Acme, shelved by Warner Bros. in 2023 for a tax write-off and later rescued by Ketchup Entertainment, opened to nearly $16 million — the strongest opening yet for a Ketchup film — while competing against Spider-Man: No Way Home and The Odyssey in theaters. The review credits director Dave Green's hybrid 2D/3D animation and live puppet approach for making the human and animated performances blend.

insights.claim: Warner Bros. shelved the completed Coyote vs. Acme in 2023 in order to take a tax write-off, a decision that sparked outrage both within the industry and among fans online.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Tax-driven shelving of finished films creates a supply of distressed content assets that smaller distributors can acquire cheaply.
insights.locator: The film is based on a well-known satirical piece

insights.claim: Ketchup Entertainment acquired and released the shelved film, and the gamble appears to be paying off with an opening weekend of nearly $16 million — the strongest opening yet for a Ketchup film — even against Spider-Man: No Way Home and The Odyssey in the theatrical mix.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A validated distressed-content acquisition model: buy a written-off title with pre-built fan awareness and capture the release upside a major studio abandoned.
insights.quote: Coyote vs. Acme racked up nearly $16 million, even with Spider-Man: No Way Home and The Odyssey still in the theatrical mix.
insights.locator: Seriously, we owe Ketchup Entertainment our gratitude

insights.claim: The author judges that the opening will not break major box office records but that the result bodes well for the film's future performance.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Modest but positive: the thesis to watch is whether legs and ancillary revenue justify further distressed-title acquisitions by small distributors.
insights.locator: OK, it won’t break any major box office records

insights.claim: The film is based on Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker satirical piece of the same name, with film development starting only in 2018 and the finished movie reaching theaters roughly three years after it was completed and shelved.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The full arc from source material to release spans decades — a reminder of how much working capital sits idle in studio development pipelines.
insights.locator: The film is based on a well-known satirical piece

insights.claim: Talent attached to the script included James Gunn, and the cast features Will Forte, John Cena, Lana Condor, Tone Bell, Martha Kelly and Luis Guzman.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Established talent attachments raise the sunk cost of a shelved film and therefore the discount at which a rescuer can acquire it.
insights.locator: Development of a film version didn’t start until 2018

insights.claim: Director Dave Green had a life-size Wile E. Coyote puppet built so actors had something to perform alongside, and shot most scenes twice — once carefully choreographed and once more spontaneously — which the reviewer credits for the seamless blend of human and animated performers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Practical on-set reference remains a cost-effective quality lever in hybrid live-action/animation production even as AI and CGI tools proliferate.

insights.claim: Green blended 3D and traditional 2D animation, reserving 3D for shots requiring better control over lighting and shadow, so the finished film still reads like a classic Looney Tunes cartoon.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Selective use of expensive 3D only where it earns its keep is a budget-discipline pattern applicable across animated production.
insights.locator: Green also opted to blend 3D and traditional 2D animation

insights.claim: Green explicitly targeted the original Looney Tunes tone as violent, irreverent, sarcastic, subversive and weird rather than saccharine, framing the film as carrying that torch.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Fidelity to the original tone rather than family-safe sanitization is being credited for the film's reception — a data point for how legacy animation IP should be revived.
insights.quote: they were sarcastic and subversive and weird
insights.locator: And the overall tone is pitched exactly right

insights.claim: The film's human characters are named in honor of Looney Tunes creators — Kevin Avery for animator Tex Avery, Sal Maltese for screenwriter Michael Maltese, and Dottie Jones for animator Chuck Jones, co-creator of Wile E. Coyote and the Road Runner.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Deep-catalog fan service is the retention mechanic these legacy-IP revivals rely on to convert nostalgia into opening-weekend attendance.
